documents.title: SAMHSA mandatory guidelines federal workplace drug testing programs

chunks.content: 1. Background The technology of oral fluid testing for misused drugs is at an advanced stage ( ; ; ; ;; ; ; ; ; ; ), but urine remains the standard matrix for drug screening in most community settings, including addiction treatment ( ; ); community corrections ( ), screening in primary care ( ; ), drug courts ( ), child protective services (Child Trends, 2017), workplace safety monitoring ( ; ), offender monitoring ( ; ), sports doping surveillance ( ; ) and other outpatient and field settings. However, oral fluid testing has several known advantages over urine analysis, specifically the elimination of privacy issues, the need to provide urine on demand, the need for restroom access, the possible need for a same-gender observer, the near-elimination of potential dilution or adulteration of specimens ( ; ; ) and the greater willingness in voluntary studies to provide oral fluid instead of urine ( ) or instead of hair ( ). Also note that primary care physicians say that urine testing for misused drugs is generally difficult to implement ( ). Oral fluid testing has been approved for clinical use by the ; ) and is included in testing recommendations by the . Although the window of detection for oral fluid has been a concern since its introduction ( ; ), more recent research based on state of the art techniques for both urine analysis and oral fluid analysis, including some controlled administration studies, indicates that the window of detection for these matrices is similar for several major drugs ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ), although relative detection windows for cocaine metabolites remain unclear ( ; ; ). Indirect evidence also suggests similar windows of detection for oral fluid and urine, in that workplace-testing programs nationally usually yield the same or higher drug positive rates for oral fluid than for urine over the last two decades ( ; ); the sometimes lower rates for urine are probably due to adulterated or diluted specimens in unobserved settings rather than the test technology. National U.S. epidemiological studies, where biomarkers from urine, blood or hair are difficult or impossible to obtain, continue to rely on self-reports of drug use, e.g., the National Household Survey ( ) and Monitoring the Future ( ), despite standing evidence that biomarkers detect considerably more drug use than self-reports (e.g., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). This is especially important because timely drug surveillance is critical for early detection and tracking of local and national drug epidemics, such as the current U.S. opiate and specifically fentanyl crises ( ; ). An important barrier to the wider use of oral fluid for testing for misused drugs is the small number of studies employing state-of-the-art testing that directly compare the results for oral fluid with urine, the most widely accepted and used matrix, for paired specimens provided by the same individuals at the same time. The most frequent type of previous study, although still few in number, compares liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS) results (a definitive test) between urine and oral fluid. Almost all of these studies have had one or more significant limitations: small subject sample sizes; limited types or numbers of drugs studied, either purposely or de facto; very low prevalence rates for many drugs; and sometimes, different testing protocols for oral fluid and urine within the same study ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). The only large sample study was . Generally, there are numerous inconsistencies in this literature, so that another broad-based, large sample study, such as the current research, is useful to conduct. It is important to note that physiological and biochemical factors may alter drug disposition in oral fluid as compared with urine, which must be considered when interpreting differences in results ( ). One finding is that parent drugs are often more detectable in oral fluid whereas their metabolites tend to be more detectable in urine ( ; ; ). One review identifies the mechanism as “renal excretion favoring water-soluble metabolite elimination, whereas oral fluid excretion favoring parent drugs capable of rapid passive diffusion across membranes” ( ). As another example, chemical properties such as acidity and glucuronidation appear to explain differences in detection rates of individual opioids and benzodiazepines in oral fluid vs. urine ( ; ). The clinical relevance of current studies comparing oral fluid with urine is limited, because none included presumptive tests (e.g., screening by immunoassay) which, followed by confirmation of positives by a definitive test, is the current standard for clinical drug monitoring. This protocol continues to be widely used despite clear clinical benefits of direct-to-definitive testing ( ; ; ; ). Although there is a body of research on the accuracy of presumptive tests in urine

properties such as acidity and glucuronidation appear to explain differences in detection rates of individual opioids and benzodiazepines in oral fluid vs. urine ( ; ). The clinical relevance of current studies comparing oral fluid with urine is limited, because none included presumptive tests (e.g., screening by immunoassay) which, followed by confirmation of positives by a definitive test, is the current standard for clinical drug monitoring. This protocol continues to be widely used despite clear clinical benefits of direct-to-definitive testing ( ; ; ; ). Although there is a body of research on the accuracy of presumptive tests in urine (e.g., ; ; ; ), there is little similar research on the accuracy of presumptive tests in oral fluid that were conducted in field settings, with two early exceptions being and . Moreover, even the research on urine is almost always focused on detection of false screening positives ( ), rather than the arguably equally important detection of false screening negatives ( ; ). Wider use of oral fluid for clinical drug monitoring would be justified if the accuracy of presumptive plus confirmation testing and/or direct-to-definitive testing were shown to be similar for urine and oral fluid, “accuracy” being defined as the minimization of both false positive and false negatives ( ). 1.1 Study Objectives. Compare the results of presumptive immunoassay screens plus LC-MS-MS confirmation of positives vs. direct-to-definitive LC-MS/MS testing for major drug classes in oral fluid and urine. Compare the results of oral fluid vs. urine for identifying specific misused drugs by direct-to-definitive LC-MS-MS testing. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1 Participants and setting The participants were individuals applying for methadone treatment in 11 clinics across 7 states (Alabama, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania). This subject population was chosen because such individuals are known to use not only opiates and opioids but also a wide range of additional types of drugs at various levels ( ; ; ). An additional advantage of studying these applicants is that they have no reason to falsify (i.e., adulterate or substitute) the urine specimen requested at clinic intake, because it is needed to establish their eligibility for treatment. In spite of this, we still checked urine creatinine and pH levels (see below). The clinics provided a convenience sample of participants based on the clinics’ interest and ability to participate in this research. Applicants were eligible for the study if they were between 18–70 years old, not applying to a methadone program directly from a residential treatment, institutional or incarceration setting; and not transferring from another methadone program, although this last criterion was relaxed towards the end of the data collection when it became clear that methadone transfers were also usually misusing drugs. Oral fluid and urine specimens needed to be collected on the first day of intake, but eventual admission to the program was not required. The data were collected between Sept. 2020 and Nov. 2022. The participants were 46.4% male, 43.2% female and 10.4% other/no answer; 69.7% White, 7.2% African American, 4.0% Latino/a, 3.4% Native American and 15.7% other/no answer. 2.2 Training and Approval All oral fluid and urine specimens and other data were collected by clinic intake counselors and nurses. The clinic staff completed human subjects protection Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI) remote trainings. Remote trainings in study procedures were conducted for each clinic by study staff. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Western Michigan University. 2.3 Study Procedures. Applicants for methadone treatment were invited to participate in the study as part of their clinic intake process. Participation was voluntary and based on verbal consent because the data collection was anonymous; no subject identifying data were collected by the study and no individually identifiable study data were shared with the clinics. Data were linked by a research number. The objective was to collect the urine and oral fluid specimens for the study within 30 minutes of each other, although data were retained if the time interval was longer (see below). Urines for the study were obtained by pipetting 5ml from the clinic’s intake urine into a separate vial. Urines were unobserved per the clinics’ standard practice. Oral fluid specimens were obtained using the Quantisal collection device ( ). Oral fluid collection required at least 10 minutes to pass after any eating or drinking by the subject before giving the specimen. The specimens were mailed overnight to Forensic Fluids Laboratories where they were frozen at −20 deg C until weekly analysis. The participants were compensated with $20 gift cards good for food (not alcohol or tobacco) at a local supermarket chain. 2.4 Toxicological analysis Oral fluid was analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and urine by homogeneous enzyme immunoassay (HEIA), the latter being a liquid reagent immunoassay which is the industry standard for urine.

Quantisal collection device ( ). Oral fluid collection required at least 10 minutes to pass after any eating or drinking by the subject before giving the specimen. The specimens were mailed overnight to Forensic Fluids Laboratories where they were frozen at −20 deg C until weekly analysis. The participants were compensated with $20 gift cards good for food (not alcohol or tobacco) at a local supermarket chain. 2.4 Toxicological analysis Oral fluid was analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and urine by homogeneous enzyme immunoassay (HEIA), the latter being a liquid reagent immunoassay which is the industry standard for urine. HEIA was not used for oral fluid because the detection limits at the time that this study was planned were not low enough to detect low concentrations of drugs in oral fluid. Both oral fluid and urine were analyzed by LC–MS-MS whether or not the screening tests were positive. Standard commercial ELISA and HEIA kits and cutoffs used are shown in . shows the linear ranges for the LC-MS-MS analyses for urine and oral fluid. The limits of quantification (LOQ) cutoffs are the low values of the ranges. We decided to use urine cutoffs at the levels recommended by the federal government ( ), since even many non-regulated employers use these guidelines ( ), although we recognize lower cutoffs are also often used both clinically and for research (e.g., ). The exceptions were morphine and codeine, where we used cutoffs less than the recommended 2000 ng/mL because we needed to measure lower concentrations for research purposes. Cutoffs for oral fluid were determined by limit of quantification (LOQ) analysis with internal standards during method validation conducted by Forensic Fluids Laboratories. For purposes of this paper, we also classified an oral fluid or urine LC-MS-MS result as positive if there was a signal for a drug (“present”) even though it could not be quantified; this avoids underestimating the prevalence of a drug when presenting qualitative results. 2.5 Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics are presented for the various drugs and drug classes tested by IA and LC-MS-MS in oral fluid and urine. Associations between test results in paired specimens are determined by cross-tabulations. The complete tabulations are not always explicitly shown, although their statistical significance as computed by the McNemar test may be. The McNemar test for asymmetry in paired data measures the degree of imbalance based on the two discordant cells in any 2 × 2 crosstabulation of test results, each classified as positive (+) or negative (−) ( ). For example, is oral positive/urine negative more or less likely than oral negative/urine positive, or are these two combinations equally likely? If not equally likely based on statistical significance of p < .05, then the prevalences of the given drug or drug class are unequal on the tests. The minimal sample size required for the McNemar test is at least ten discordant pairs, assuming Yates correction. Cohen’s kappa (k) is a summary measure of agreement between the results of test #1 and test #2, each classified as positive vs. negative, with k = 0 indicating agreement expected by chance alone (based on the marginal distributions) and k = 1 indicating perfect agreement ( ). Values between 0 and 1 indicate increasing agreement beyond chance (although less than .60 is characterized as “weak” agreement) and values less than 0, which are rare in actual research, indicate less agreement than expected by chance alone. All statistical analyses were conducted with SPSS version 27. 2.6. Specimen validity parameters Creatinine was measured in all urine specimens. 22 participants tested < 20 ng/mL which is possibly indicative of dilution ( ), but in addition to participants having no incentive to do this, all those with low creatinine also tested positive for multiple drugs in urine; thus all those with ostensibly low creatine levels were retained in the analysis. No participants tested >300 ng/ml creatinine, which would be indicative of an adulterated specimen. The number of participants with paired oral fluid and urine specimens was 1099, of whom the time interval between the urine and oral fluid specimens could be calculated for 1076. This time interval was <30 minutes for 97.9% of the sample. Of the remaining, one extreme outlier subject (545 minutes) was excluded. Analyses were then conducted to determine whether there were any associations between time interval (classified as <30 minutes vs. >30 minutes) and disagreement on screening test results (classed as positive vs. negative) for major drug categories: opiates, cocaine, amphetamine-type stimulants and benzodiazepines; there were no statistically significant differences (p > .05). In addition, all urine pH values were in the acceptable range (> 3 and < 11) according to the vendor. 3. Results 3.1. In addition, all urine pH values were in the acceptable range (> 3 and < 11) according to the vendor. 3. Results 3.1. Objective 1 The prevalences of drug use as measured by 12 presumptive immunoassay (IA) tests, with IA positives both unconfirmed and confirmed by LC-MS-MS, are shown in columns one and two for oral fluid and columns four and five for urine in . The unconfirmed results are for the record only, because IA plus confirmation of positives is the standard clinical protocol. The initial IA test results for amphetamines and methamphetamines were combined into one category, “amphetamine-type stimulants,” because amphetamines, while subject to misuse directly, are also the main metabolites of methamphetamines, and the correlation between test results for amphetamines and methamphetamines is very high. A participant was classified as positive for amphetamine-type stimulants if they were positive on either the amphetamine or methamphetamine immunoassays. Statistical comparisons could not be made for ketamine and synthetic cannabinoids because of insufficient positives; this results in subsequent analyses for ten drug classes. As expected, shows that confirmed IA prevalences are the same or less than unconfirmed for both oral fluid and urine due to the elimination of false IA positives. Confirmed IA prevalences for urine are significantly higher than for oral fluid for 7 out of the 10 drug classes where comparisons can be made - benzodiazepines, cannabis, cocaine, methadone, opiates, oxycodone and tramadol (p < .05, McNemar’s test), whereas prevalence by oral fluid is never higher for any class. The third and sixth columns in show the prevalences of the drug classes as measured by LC-MS-MS for oral fluid and urine, respectively. That is, a positive result for a drug class was indicated if any specific drug belonging to that class was found to be positive by LC-MS-MS. As expected, prevalences by LC-MS-MS were either the same or higher than prevalences by confirmed IA for both oral fluid and urine due to the elimination of false IA negatives. Prevalences by LC-MS-MS were significantly higher for urine than oral fluid for two drug classes, cocaine and methadone, and significantly higher for oral fluid than urine for two drug classes, buprenorphine and tramadol. Columns one and two in show the magnitudes of the increases in drug class prevalences as measured by LC-MS-MS vs. confirmed IA for oral fluid and urine, respectively. Magnitude is defined as the ratio of LC-MS-MS prevalence to confirmed IA prevalence. This ratio averaged over 10 drug classes is 1.40 for oral fluid and 1.05 for urine. For oral fluid, column one in shows that the largest differences in drug prevalences between LC-MS-MS and confirmed IA are for tramadol, benzodiazepines, and oxycodone. For urine, column two in shows the largest differences are for methadone, benzodiazepines oxycodone, although the differences are very small. Column three in quantifies the differences in drug class prevalences by LC-MS-MS between oral fluid and urine that are seen in . For example, cocaine is 1.39 times as likely to be found in urine than in oral fluid, whereas buprenorphine was 0.7 times as likely to be found in urine than in oral fluid. Prevalences by LC-MS-MS are significantly higher in urine than oral fluid for two drug classes (cocaine and methadone) and significantly higher in oral fluid than urine for two drug classes (buprenorphine and tramadol). There is no overall significant difference in drug use prevalence between oral fluid and urine when averaged over all 10 possible drug classes. 3.2. Objective 2 Prevalences by LC-MS-MS for specific drugs within classes, separately for oral fluid and urine, are presented in . also shows the degree of agreement between oral fluid and urine in the sample for the drug classes and specific drugs. All drugs included in the LC-MS-MS panel that are relevant to the IA screens are shown, except for 19 synthetic cannabinoids that were uniformly negative; two others with positives are shown. indicates which specific drugs might explain the differences in prevalence of certain drug classes between oral fluid and urine. For example, urine testing appears to be uniquely sensitive to oxazepam (Serax).. Further interpretation of the differences between oral fluid and urine test results take place in the Discussion. 4. Discussion Within a confirmed IA testing protocol, urine appears to have some advantage over oral fluid in sensitivity for detecting most of the major drug classes, because most of the screens focus on metabolites of the active drugs, the former being more persistent in urine, with the caveat that this presumes universal validity of the oral fluid and urine specimens. The present study meets this condition, and oral fluid collection can always be observed, but of course the validity of urine specimens is often problematic in routine clinical and laboratory donation settings. Perhaps the latter is reason enough to prefer oral fluid testing in many settings, especially since the differences in accuracy of oral fluid vs. urine testing as measured by differences in drug prevalences are usually not large and can be mitigated to a considerable extent by conducting multiple tests. This deserves some elaboration. The results of the present study as well as most previous studies with paired oral fluid/urine specimens are based on a single test (donation) per subject, a situation unlikely to occur clinically, where multiple tests over a relatively short period are either available or could be obtained, e.g., in methadone treatment clinics or chronic pain clinics. (In fact, there are cautions about making major clinical decisions based on a single toxicology.) While a patient would be less likely to be positive on any single less sensitive test, several such tests within a defined time period would likely identify as many persons with substance use disorders as a single more sensitive test. This is true theoretically and could be verified empirically by the data collected by at least two previous studies. These are , who have oral fluid and urine test data from 5,061 paired tests conducted for 2,746 unique patients and , who have 1,544 paired tests conducted for 133 unique patients; however, such analysis was not performed. Note that multiple oral fluid testing is especially feasible (though there might be increased cost), which could compensate for its lower sensitivity as compared with urine testing for certain classes of drugs. Thus, differences in sensitivity between oral fluid and urine testing of the magnitudes observed for most drug classes in this study should not unduly influence the choice of test matrix for clinical monitoring purposes. This suggestion holds for both confirmed IA and direct-to-definitive testing protocols. We will now discuss differences between oral fluid and urine in direct-to-definitive LC-MS-MS results as shown in . Although there is no difference in detection of amphetamine-type stimulants as a class, amphetamines specifically are more detectable in urine than oral fluid. This may be because amphetamines, in addition to being ingested directly, are also the main metabolites of methamphetamine, and urine tends to be superior for detecting persistent metabolites. Methamphetamine (“crystal meth”) is a frequently misused drug equally prevalent in oral fluid and urine. The study also tested for several other drugs among amphetamine-type stimulants – MDEA, MDMA, phentermine – but found only one positive. MDMA (Ecstasy, Molly) particularly has been prominent on the electronic music club scene among young people ( ), but apparently has not penetrated into the population of this study. In the benzodiazepine category, a large majority of the positives by LC-MS-MS are attributable to alprazolam (Xanax) and oxazepam (Serax). However, oral fluid appears almost entirely insensitive to oxazepam, whereas it is more sensitive than urine to alprazolam. Previous research has reported that urine is generally more sensitive to detection of benzodiazepines than oral fluid ( ; ), but our finding is that the preferred matrix seems to depend on the particular benzodiazepine. Buprenorphine as a category was more frequently detected in oral fluid, although only the parent buprenorphine was found significantly more frequently in oral fluid; agreement beyond chance between oral fluid and urine was low (kappa = .52). This differs from the findings by and where buprenorphine was more prevalent in urine. In particular, found 90.5% positive for the buprenorphine parent by urine and 78.9% by oral fluid. However, this previous research employed higher cutoffs for oral fluid and lower cutoffs for urine, which could easily account for difference with the current study. For instance, 60% of the buprenorphine parent positives in the current study showed concentrations below the 1.0 ng/mL cutoff employed by . If had been able to employ a lower cutoff of 0.1 ng/mL as in our study, the difference between the matrices might well have been eliminated. A similar conclusion could be reached with respect to

in urine. In particular, found 90.5% positive for the buprenorphine parent by urine and 78.9% by oral fluid. However, this previous research employed higher cutoffs for oral fluid and lower cutoffs for urine, which could easily account for difference with the current study. For instance, 60% of the buprenorphine parent positives in the current study showed concentrations below the 1.0 ng/mL cutoff employed by . If had been able to employ a lower cutoff of 0.1 ng/mL as in our study, the difference between the matrices might well have been eliminated. A similar conclusion could be reached with respect to . This also points out the potentially important role of cutoffs in interpreting the findings of different studies relating to matrix differences; studies with varied findings should not necessarily be interpreted as either “right” or “wrong.” Although agreement on cannabis detection was only moderate (kappa = .65), there was no significant difference in prevalence between oral fluid and urine. Using the same measures, found higher prevalence of cannabis in urine, but that study’s higher cutoff for delta-9 THC (2.0 ng/mL) for oral fluid may explain the difference in findings. At our study’s cutoff of 0.1 ng/mL, 42% of the positives were between 0.1 – 2.0 ng/mL. Thus, if had been able to employ our cutoff, it is likely considerably more positives would have been obtained for oral fluid in their study. Cocaine as a category was more likely to be detected in urine, which was attributable to the greater likelihood of finding benzoylecgonine (BZE) in urine, the major metabolite of cocaine, due its now well-known longer elimination time in urine (Huestis, 2009). There was no significant difference in detecting the parent drug, cocaine. Research has been inconsistent about whether oral fluid or urine is the preferred matrix for detecting cocaine use ( ; ; ; ). found higher prevalence of cocaine/BZE in oral fluid than in urine, but the parent cocaine was only measured in oral fluid. The present study, which includes the largest number of cocaine/BZE positives in the relevant literature other than , shows that for unselected persons with substance use disorders, urine is at least slightly more sensitive than oral fluid to cocaine use, due to the wider window of detection of BZE in urine. This may have been assumed previously, but until now had not been statistically demonstrated. Overall, fentanyl as a category was equally prevalent in oral fluid and urine, although the parent fentanyl had higher prevalence in oral fluid and the major metabolite norfentanyl had higher prevalence in urine. In comparison, , based on a smaller number of positives, found fentanyl (defined as detection of the parent or metabolite) to be more prevalent in oral fluid (2.9%) vs. urine (2.0%), although this small difference might no longer be statistically significant if adjustment were made for autocorrelation, i.e., multiple test runs on the same individuals. More recently, again for a smaller sample of paired specimens, fentanyl was detected more often in urine (19.0%) than oral fluid (14.8 %), but “fentanyl” was defined differently for the two matrices – the urine test included norfentanyl but the oral fluid test did not, which clearly affects the matrix comparison ( ). Our fentanyl results are based on a large number of fentanyl positives due to the emergence of the national fentanyl epidemic during the period of data collection. Because our sampling recruited individuals with opioid use disorder, it would be expected that they would be prime consumers of fentanyl now that it has become readily available as a street drug ( ). Our findings have important implications for tracking the fentanyl epidemic in real-time epidemiological research using oral fluid as a highly feasible method of specimen collection. Ketamine was not a prominent street drug at the time of the study, although its therapeutic applications seem to be increasing recently, which through diversion might make it more available as a street drug in the future (e.g., ). Both the parent drug methadone and especially its main metabolite 2-ethylene-1,5-dimethyl-3,3-diphenylpyrrolidine (EDDP) were more likely to be detected in urine. This is based on by far the largest number of methadone positives for oral fluid and urine reported in the literature to date. The concentrations found in our study were consistent with those previously reported for individuals receiving methadone maintenance treatment ( ). The higher prevalence of EDDP in urine is most likely due to its long excretion time. Nonetheless, for the purpose of monitoring therapeutic ingestion of methadone, there would be little difference based on combined results for both the parent methadone and EDDP – 34% positive for urine and 29% for oral fluid. As for the relatively high prevalence of methadone, this is likely due to participants transferring to several of the study clinics from other methadone programs and to

The higher prevalence of EDDP in urine is most likely due to its long excretion time. Nonetheless, for the purpose of monitoring therapeutic ingestion of methadone, there would be little difference based on combined results for both the parent methadone and EDDP – 34% positive for urine and 29% for oral fluid. As for the relatively high prevalence of methadone, this is likely due to participants transferring to several of the study clinics from other methadone programs and to use of “street” methadone ( ; ). However, they almost always also tested positive for a variety of other drugs. Opiates as a class were equally likely to be detected in oral fluid and urine, but there was variation between oral fluid and urine depending on the specific opiate. Oral fluid was considerably more sensitive to the presence of 6-monoacetylmorphine (6-MAM), a unique metabolite of heroin ( ), which is a consistent previous finding ( ; ; ; ). Oral fluid was also more sensitive to the presence of codeine (similar to ) and hydrocodone (Vicodin). When the parent hydrocodone and its metabolite norhydrocodone are combined as indicators of hydrocodone ingestion, hydrocodone remains significantly more prevalent in oral fluid. Urine appears to be more sensitive to hydromorphone (Dilaudid) and there was no difference between the matrices on morphine, which is a major metabolite of many opiates, and likely accounts for the overall finding of no difference between the matrices on the prevalence of opiates. Previous research has been inconsistent on this, with reporting morphine more prevalent in urine but in oral fluid. report results similar to ours for hydromorphone and morphine. Oxycodone as a category was equally likely to be present in oral fluid and urine, although there was a non-significant tendency for the oxycodone parent to be found more often in oral fluid and the metabolite oxymorphone more often in urine, which is consistent with the report by for a larger sample of oxycodone and oxymorphone positives. Note that oxymorphone (Opana) may also be detected as the primary drug ingested, although the extended release version was withdrawn from the market in 2017. Tramadol was more likely to be detected in oral fluid than urine, which is consistent with . Overall, our results regarding relative prevalence rates, based on a large sample, indicate oral fluid and urine are about equally efficient for monitoring overall opiate and opioid (synthetic opiate) use, unless there is a specific drug of therapeutic, research or epidemiological interest that needs to be targeted. This is most pertinent for heroin, where oral fluid is substantially superior to urine for the detection of one of its unique metabolites, 6-MAM. The two studies with the largest samples of paired oral fluid/urine specimens in the literature – the current study and - yielded generally consistent findings for direct-to-definitive testing for a wide range of drugs. Certain significant differences, e.g., for buprenorphine and cannabis, can apparently be explained by differences in cutoff levels. 4.1. Study Limitations The findings are for the specified laboratory-based IA tests; this could vary if different IA tests including point of care (POC) tests with different sensitivities and specificities were to be used. The potential benefit of direct-to-definitive testing in identifying specific drugs for which there are no generally used or practical IA screens was not addressed by this paper, but should be considered when making a decision about implementing direct-to-definitive testing in a clinical setting or for epidemiological purposes. The clinical implications of the study are limited by the design of a single test run per participant, as explained above. Not all drug classes of interest are well-represented, e.g., synthetic cannabinoids, due to rarity of use in the study’s participant population. The greater expense of direct-to-definitive as compared with presumptive with confirmation testing and its implications for clinical use were not examined by the study, although the difference in expense seems to be narrowing ( ). The study did not report drug concentrations in oral fluid and urine, which will be presented as a separate topic in a subsequent paper. However, in a few instances reference to concentrations was made to help in interpreting the qualitative test results. As in most previous similar studies, LC-MS-MS positives were determined by the limits of the technology; the study was not designed to investigate optimal cutoffs for clinical purposes. Finally, there is evidence that provider education is essential to properly interpret direct to definitive drug test results ( ; ) 5. Conclusions Urine analysis showed some technical advantage over oral fluid in sensitivity to several classes of drugs within a confirmed IA testing protocol, but this may be outweighed if there is reason to believe that tampering with urine

to concentrations was made to help in interpreting the qualitative test results. As in most previous similar studies, LC-MS-MS positives were determined by the limits of the technology; the study was not designed to investigate optimal cutoffs for clinical purposes. Finally, there is evidence that provider education is essential to properly interpret direct to definitive drug test results ( ; ) 5. Conclusions Urine analysis showed some technical advantage over oral fluid in sensitivity to several classes of drugs within a confirmed IA testing protocol, but this may be outweighed if there is reason to believe that tampering with urine specimens is a significant problem. Direct to definitive testing by LC-MS-MS yielded significantly higher prevalences for most drug classes than did confirmed IA, although the differences were more pronounced for oral fluid than urine. Direct-to-definitive testing yielded higher prevalences by urine for two and higher prevalences by oral fluid for two, out of 10 drug classes. However, oral fluid has a significant advantage specifically in detection of heroin use. In both confirmed IA and direct-to-definitive testing protocols, multiple oral fluid tests that are feasible in many clinical settings could compensate for the slightly lower sensitivity of oral fluid for certain drug classes. This study, based on one of the largest paired samples of oral fluid and urine specimens, with no incentive or reason for participants to tamper with their urine specimens, provides new information to assist treatment administrators, clinicians and researchers to decide on the optimal drug testing protocol for their specific environments.

documents.title: SAMHSA clinical drug testing primary care opioid management

chunks.content: Introduction People who inject drugs (PWID) have a high number of co-occurring medical conditions. In a large retrospective review of patients with active substance use, found hypertension (47%), tobacco use (46%), depression (43%), hyperlipidemia (24%), hepatitis C (HCV) (22%), and diabetes mellitus (21%) were among the most frequently recorded comorbid conditions. In a random sample of individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD), 91% had at least one documented chronic illness, with a mean of 2.6 chronic illnesses, and among individuals receiving methadone, 68% were prescribed at least one additional medication for the management of their chronic illness ( ). Further, one longitudinal cohort study of PWID identified that individuals with a detectable HIV viral load were more likely to have uncontrolled comorbid diseases like diabetes or hypertension ( ). Multimorbid diseases in this population are largely undiagnosed or undertreated ( ; ). Government organizations and national interest groups concerned with the health and wellness of PWID often limit the scope of their guidelines to harm reduction and infectious disease treatment and prevention. For example, guidelines from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for primary and preventative care of PWID focuses on infectious diseases, namely HIV, HCV, hepatitis B (HBV), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and tuberculosis (TB); these guidelines only mention the importance of referral and engagement in primary care for integrated services ( ). Recommendations for engaging individuals with substance use disorders in primary care for treatment of comorbid conditions are lacking, and often focus mostly on the delivery of safer use supplies via syringe access programs embedded within these sites ( ). The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) has offered funding to health care organizations that integrate mental health and primary care but with little attention paid to PWID ( ). An increasing number of providers are prepared to treat opioid use disorder (OUD) with evidence-based medications in the primary care setting. The 2016 Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA) allowed nurse practitioners and physicians associates to prescribe buprenorphine and expanded the accessibility and availability of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD). In addition, as x-waiver requirements continue to loosen and clinicians are able to treat limited numbers of patients with buprenorphine without completing onerous training, primary care providers can play a larger role in managing the holistic care of individuals with OUD ( ). Moving OUD treatment out of specialized substance use disorder treatment centers and into primary care is important as the healthcare needs of this population extend beyond treatment with MOUD and sequela related to injection drug use ( ). Existing literature has highlighted the multitude of reasons why people who use drugs, especially PWID, avoid healthcare environments. These reasons include previous negative experiences with stigmatizing healthcare providers and receipt of low-quality care that failed to address their needs ( ; ; ). Addressing these and other barriers to healthcare engagement and providing quality primary care to people who inject drugs is vital to improving chronic illness management in this population. In addition, providing positive and affirming healthcare experiences can counter the numerous documented and undocumented negative experiences that have historically pushed people who use drugs away from healthcare environments. Clinicians aiming to treat PWID in primary care settings may benefit from frameworks identifying barriers and facilitators to care engagement among marginalized populations. The Behavioral Model for Vulnerable populations, adapted from the Andersen Model for Healthcare Utilization, examines Predisposing, Enabling, Need, and Health Behavior characteristics associated with healthcare utilization and engagement ( ; ; ). Predisposing factors are individual characteristics and include age, race, gender, education, relationship status, and sexual orientation. Enabling characteristics are organizational and financial factors including health insurance status, health service resources, and region of residence. Need characteristics refer to those that are both perceived by an individual and those evaluated by healthcare providers. Finally, health behaviors are actions taken by PWID that inhibit or enable their ability to engage in their healthcare. This framework is useful to characterize the factors associated with healthcare utilization and engagement for this marginalized population. The purpose of this review, guided by the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, is to identify the barriers and facilitators to primary care engagement for PWID. Our review addresses a gap in knowledge regarding factors associated with primary care engagement among individuals with active injection drug use. Findings can be used to inform clinical interventions and future research to improve healthcare engagement among this population. Methods Search Strategy This review utilized the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) checklist for its organization and reported elements ( ). We searched PubMed, CINAHL, and EMBASE using a combination of MeSH (or CINAHL/EMBASE equivalent) for articles published between 2000–2020. Keywords searches combined common terms for 1) engagement in care (patient participation, patient acceptance of healthcare, patient compliance, utilization), 2) intravenous substance use, and 3) primary healthcare (primary, preventative health, primary prevention, secondary prevention, tertiary prevention). A comprehensive search strategy is listed in . We also reviewed reference lists from studies in the full test phase for additional studies that met inclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria The outcome of interest was engagement in primary care. Articles that reported a study population of people who actively inject drugs (within the past 12 months) and outcomes related to engagement in primary care were included. We define “engagement” broadly to encompass a wide range of outcomes. Previous literature has highlighted that people who use drugs may avoid healthcare environments due to past negative experiences. Thus, any level of engagement, even just receipt of medication, represents an opportunity to provide a positive healthcare experience and potentially change an individual’s perception of the benefits of engaging with healthcare providers. We characterized indicators for engagement in healthcare by any of the following outcomes: 1) Visits with a healthcare provider for disease diagnosis or management, including reported patient-provider relationship; 2) Receipt of or adherence to medications or health services, for example receipt and adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV; 3) Control of diagnosed disease, such as blood pressure control or curative treatment for Hepatitis C. Articles with study populations only partially made up of active PWID were considered for inclusion if they stratified analysis to include effect estimates for people who actively inject. We excluded studies focused on people reporting a history of injection drug use (but no current injection drug use), and those that did not explicitly measure injection drug use. Studies were also excluded if they did not explicitly measure engagement outcomes with PWID or did not report any domains related to engagement in primary care. Review articles, conference abstracts and qualitative studies were excluded. Articles without full-text unavailability or that were published in a language other than English were also excluded. Finally, given differences in healthcare delivery systems, study populations outside the United States were excluded. Data extraction Guided by the theoretical domains of the Behavior Model of Healthcare Utilization, we categorized studies by factors associated with the predisposing, enabling, need, or health behavior domains; studies could include factors that are in multiple domains of the framework. ‘Predisposing characteristics’ are existing characteristics that are not directly responsible for an individual’s decision to engage in care (ex. age, gender, race); ‘enabling conditions’ are facilitators or barriers to care engagement outside the individual’s control (ex. stigma, racism, structural barriers, delivery of salient services, etc.); ‘need conditions’ are divided into actual need (presence of a medical condition) and perceived need (the level to which patients desire care engagement); ‘health behaviors’ included substance use patterns and harm reduction uptake ( ; ; ). Two authors (OH and KT) conducted data extraction and quality assessments based on published guidelines ( ; ). Results A total of 801 articles were identified using the search terms in PubMed, CINAHL, and EMBASE, 73 of which were duplicates ( ). OH and KT screened 728 titles and abstracts for relevance. An additional five were included from reference lists of articles reviewed in the full text phase. OH and KT reviewed 132 full texts for inclusion, with JF adjudicating one disagreement. A total of 23 articles were included in the final review ( ). displays the study characteristics for each included article. The majority (56%) were cross-sectional design or a cross-sectional secondary analysis of cohort or randomized control studies. The rest were from cohort studies (28%) or program evaluations (16%). Most articles (56%) were rated as ‘Good’ quality, with eleven articles rated as ‘Fair’ or ‘Poor’ ( ). That study, however, only displayed percentages of person-time stratified by race and gender with ART and viral load outcomes, without conducting relevant multivariable analysis or testing for differences between the groups. Race and Ethnicity Two studies measured engagement outcomes among PWID by race and ethnicity. One demonstrated that over 3 years, Black (aPR 1.07; 95% CI 1.02–1.13) and Hispanic (aPR 1.10; 95% CI 1.02–1.18) PWID significantly increased ART initiation ( ). Another study found Hispanic (aOR 2.28; 1.37–3.82) and non-Hispanic Black (aOR 2.22; 95% CI 1.71–2.87) PWID had greater odds of having a HIV prevention discussion with their healthcare provider at their most recent visit compared to non-Hispanic white PWID ( ). Education Results regarding education and engagement were inconsistent. Two studies were mixed on findings regarding education and medication adherence, specifically ART use. found significantly lower odds of ART initiation among PWID with less than an 8 th grade education (aOR 0.54; 95% CI 0.35–0.85) compared to PWID with an 8 th grade education or higher. Conversely, another cohort study found that over a 3-year period, PWID with a high school or less education significantly increased ART use (aPR 1.10; 95% CI 1.05–1.15), but the association was not true for PWID with a high school education or higher ( ). Regarding uptake of infectious disease screening, one study found PWID with a high school or higher education had significantly higher odds of testing for Hepatitis C in the last year (aOR 1.19; 95% CI 1.4–2.5) compared to PWID who had not attained high school education ( ). With regards to patient-provider outcomes, one study found PWID with a high school or less education had significantly higher odds of a preventative healthcare discussion with their providers at the most recent care visit (aOR 1.86; 95% CI 1.27–2.72) compared to education beyond high school ( ). Age Two studies measured the effect of age on ART use. Both showed that older age was significantly associated with ART use in multivariable models ( ; ). Additionally, found that age greater than or equal to 39 was associated with increased primary care utilization in a multivariable model, compared to age less than 39 (aOR 1.82; 95% CI 1.09–3.05). Enabling factors associated with healthcare engagement Health insurance and financial barriers Five studies that examined the effect of having health insurance on a measure of engagement in care, and all showed a significant positive association. Multiple studies demonstrated a significant increase in primary care visits for PWID with health insurance compared to uninsured PWID, with point estimate odds ranging from 2.00 to 2.58 ( ; ; ). Having health insurance was also significantly associated with increases in ART uptake ( ; ). One study grouped lack of health insurance, inability to afford co-pay, and indicators of a poor relationship with provider, including not feeling comfortable with provider, scared to see a provider, and not having an established provider into one variable of “barriers to seeing a primary care provider (PCP).” As such, PWID who had a higher mean number of these barriers were less likely to see a PCP in the last year (p<0.001) ( ). High cost was the most frequently reported barrier to accessing healthcare in one study focused on commercial sex workers who inject drugs ( ). Location of services Three studies reported quality measurements related to co-location of primary care services with another service salient to PWID (i.e. hepatitis C treatment or buprenorphine). Results were promising with high retention in care (61%) with buprenorphine services and high success for hepatitis C treatment (98%) when co-located in the primary care setting ( ; ). In another study, women who injected drugs reported strong desire for receipt of primary care at needle exchange (72%), supervised consumption sites (78%), and though mobile care (70%) ( ). In another study, women who injected drugs reported strong desire for receipt of primary care at needle exchange (72%), supervised consumption sites (78%), and though mobile care (70%) ( ). These studies, however, reported on care outcomes without exploring differences by individual or structural factors, and only conducted descriptive analyses. One additional study with comparison groups found that location of usual care differed significantly; PWID living with HCV were more likely to report utilizing the emergency room over primary care compared to HCV antibody negative PWID (p=0.02) ( ). Patient-provider relationship and substance use stigma The two articles that examined the effect of patient-provider relationship on engagement in care both indicated a that positive patient-provider relationship was associated with increased ART initiation (aOR 1.45; 95% CI 1.09–1.93) ( ), while a lack of rapport with their primary care provider was associated with not testing for HCV in the last 12 months (p=0.02) ( ). With respect to the relationship with their PCP, PWID who reported a higher mean of harm reduction topics discussed with their PCP (p<0.001) and those whose PCP was aware of their substance use (p<0.001) were more likely to have a PCP visit in the last year ( ). Housing Both articles that examined the effect of housing found a deleterious effect of homelessness on engagement in care ( ; ). Among those living with HIV, those actively engaged in injection drug use were more likely to report homelessness compared to those who were not actively injecting (p<0.001); active PWID in that study were found to have worse health outcomes, even when utilizing HIV primary care ( ). Conversely, stable housing was significantly associated with uptake of ART (aOR 2.05; 95% CI 1.11–3.77) compared to PWID reporting unstable housing ( ). Peer norms One study demonstrated the positive influence of peers on engagement. Peers acted as social support during substance use disorder treatment and helped improve ART adherence and clinic appointment attendance ( ). Findings were limited to 14 patients in this feasibility study, but this peer support model demonstrated success in improving care engagement among PWID. Participants receiving peer support kept 84% of scheduled primary care appointments, and the intervention led to sustained ART adherence (90% of participants) and enrollment in substance use disorder treatment (75% of participants) ( ). Need factors associated with healthcare engagement Perceived need One study found that PWID with increased healthcare utilization (increased number of visits) had significantly increased odds of taking ART 6 months later (aOR 1.44; 95% CI 1.09–1.91) compared to PWID with less utilization ( ). Another study noted that rating HIV care as ‘very important’ (aOR 1.77; 1.31, 2.37) was significantly associated with having a HIV prevention discussion with a healthcare provider compared those who rated HIV care as less than ‘very important’ on a 4-point Likert scale ( ). Actual need In two studies, HIV disease stage was significantly associated with engagement in healthcare. PWID with a CD4 counts <350 were more likely than those with higher counts to be taking ART at the 6 month follow up visit (aOR 1.65; 95% CI 1.23–2.22), while those with CD4 counts >= 200 had more visits with a primary care provider than those with lower counts (aOR 1.64; 95% CI 1.10–2.46) ( ; ). Four studies measured diagnosed chronic health conditions among PWID. One study demonstrated that people actively injecting drugs were significantly more likely to be diagnosed with chronic infectious diseases (HIV, HCV, Hepatitis B) compared to past injection drug users (p<0.001) ( ). In another study, PWID living with HIV had 2 times higher adjusted odds of a major depression diagnosis compared to people living with HIV who did not report active injection drug use (95% CI 1.75–2.73) ( ). An additional study found that PWID with a higher reported mean of conditions treated by their PCP were more likely to have seen their PCP in the last year (p=0.04) ( ). Finally, one study measured syndemic psychological and structural distress among PWID, finding that higher levels of psychological distress were significantly associated with not taking ART (aOR 2.47; 95% CI 1.41–4.30), poor adherence to ART (aOR 2.56; 95% CI 1.07–2.63), and a detectable viral load (aOR 2.24; 95% CI 1.18–4.27) ( ). Discussion This systematic review identified factors related to engagement in primary care among people actively injecting drugs. Among the 23 included articles, the majority were observational studies utilizing descriptive designs. Although the assessment of evidence was primarily rated ‘good’, this review identifies a significant need to improve our understanding of primary care engagement for PWID. Two prior systematic reviews have been conducted with similar populations. conducted a systematic review that used the Andersen Healthcare Utilization Model to assess utilization of hospital-based outpatient services among people living with HIV. However, this review did not specifically focus on PWID. Another review conducted using literature published between 2000–2010 examined models of primary care delivery and the acceptability of these services by PWID ( ), but had an international focus and also did not restrict to active injection drug use. Additionally, , published an article related to primary care engagement among PWID, but did not take a systematic approach and only reported clinical care recommendations. Guided by the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, we synthesized factors within the model’s four domains, and their impact on engagement in primary care outcomes ( ). From the Enabling domain, patient-provider relationship emerged as a strong factor related to care engagement: across all the studies reviewed, positive patient-provider relationship was associated with greater engagement and negative relationships associated with less engagement. These findings were consistent with the broader literature of chronic disease management showing positive patient-provider relationships associated with higher levels of care engagement ( ; ). Co-location of services also emerged as a facilitator to primary care engagement, but studies associated with this finding were not highly rated due to limitations related to statistical analysis. Other international studies with PWID have also identified provision of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) in the primary care setting as a factor correlated to engagement in healthcare, though these international studies did not meet criteria for inclusion in this review ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Finally, current insurance status was associated with healthcare engagement across the five studies that measured it, but only two were published on data collected after the Affordable Care Act. These finding suggest that linkage to healthcare insurance could be more salient to healthcare engagement with the expansion of health insurance. One recent study found that PWID in Medicaid expansion states were more likely to have insurance (aPR 2.3; 95% CI 2.0–2.6) and have a usual source of healthcare (aPR 1.5; 95% CI 1.3–1.9) ( ) than PWID in non-expansion states. This study was not included in our analysis due to the authors’ definition of PWID including individuals reporting non-injection opioid use. Predisposing factors were not well measured or well represented across the studies with a few exceptions. Only one study stratified analysis by sex or gender but did not conduct analyses or provide effect estimates of engagement in care ( ). As a whole, measures and comparisons of race and ethnicity were also inconsistent. While differences in race as a predisposing factor were reported, little can be drawn from them without reported effect estimates and improved study design. Andro- and ethnocentrism was evident since many studies had samples that were over 50% male and rarely had balance in racial and ethnic groups, which also limits conclusions regarding sex, gender, race and ethnicity. While differences in race as a predisposing factor were reported, little can be drawn from them without reported effect estimates and improved study design. Andro- and ethnocentrism was evident since many studies had samples that were over 50% male and rarely had balance in racial and ethnic groups, which also limits conclusions regarding sex, gender, race and ethnicity. Evidence from the need domain described the complicated nature of care engagement for PWID. Studies demonstrated high burden of multimorbidity, difficulty engaging with accessible healthcare services that meet perceived needs, and the competing nature of active substance use with engagement in primary care. Health behaviors were most consistently measured across studies, with strong evidence that active injecting was a salient barrier to care engagement. This could be an area where clinicians can better assess injecting practices and provide harm reduction services in the primary care setting ( ) or co-locate health services within harm reduction centers ( ). There were limitations to this study. Filters on publishing date were applied to this systematic review, though we reviewed evidence over a 20-year period. This introduces bias as secular changes in healthcare policy and service access contribute greatly to healthcare engagement. Additionally, engagement in healthcare as an outcome proved difficult for data synthesis, as outcomes for engagement are wider ranging than healthcare utilization measures alone. This broader definition, however, allows for more nuanced analysis and understanding of healthcare needs of this population. Finally, many studies were excluded because they did not explicitly measure active injection drug use or stratify their results based on active injecting. Future studies with PWID would benefit from collecting and reporting on active versus historical injection drug use and incorporating a clear conceptual framework to define healthcare engagement outcomes. Clinical Relevance Nursing plays an important role in healthcare engagement for PWID. Recent evidence has shown that nurse-led clinics and the expansion of medications for opioid use disorder address critical gaps in these essential services for PWID, particularly in rural areas ( ; ; ; ; ). Additionally, nurses and nurse case managers working in the primary care setting play a critical role in addressing holistic care needs of patients, including some barriers identified by this review, and can engage PWID in primary care long term ( ; ). Overall, nurses in the primary care setting play an important role in addressing barriers to care engagement, improving access to essential substance use and primary care services, and developing meaningful patient-nurse and patient-care team relationships. Conclusions Although the preponderance of evidence is mixed, we identified several factors as barriers or facilitators to engagement in primary care for PWID. Given the ongoing overdose crisis, we must develop evidence-based strategies to engage individuals in the primary care setting for needs extending beyond infectious disease prevention and management and treatment of substance use disorders ( ). Clinical practice and research should continue to consider patients and research participants’ aggregate needs rather than the sum of their disease parts. While most of the studies here focused on engagement in HIV and substance use disorder care within the primary care setting, our findings can direct future research focused on PWID’s engagement in primary care broadly.
